source.title: Easy-to-Hard Generalization: Scalable Alignment Beyond Human Supervision
source.authors: Zhi-Qing Sun; Longhui Yu; Yikang Shen; Weiyang Liu; Yiming Yang; S. Welleck; Chuang Gan

page_placements.theme: Easy-to-hard generalization (training on easy or decomposed tasks, or with easy-trained reward models, tested on hard ones)

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses Burns et al.'s weak-to-strong work as an analogy, but explicitly studies a different setup: easy-task human/simulated-human supervision and reward-model evaluation or optimization on hard tasks. Its results do not test weak-model labels beating the weak supervisor or any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The study reports easy-to-hard results for generators and reward models, but those results use easy-task solutions or process labels rather than labels produced by a weaker supervisor. It also does not measure PGR. Results cited from other papers and scores appearing only in figures without a usable text value are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests easy-to-hard generalization: generators and reward models trained on human or simulated-human labels for easy MATH (level 1-3) and APPS (Introductory) problems, then evaluated on hard problems. No student is fine-tuned on a weaker model's labels, there is no weak-supervisor baseline, and the authors explicitly decline to compute PGR (Sec. 3.5). Burns et al. is cited only as a contrasting analogy (Fig. 1, Sec. 2.1), so no claim version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that evaluators (PRMs, ORMs and OPRMs) trained only on easy tasks generalize to hard tasks better than generators do. They argue these evaluators can raise hard-task generator performance via reranking or RL, reporting 34.0% (7b RL) and 52.5% (34b reranking@1024) on MATH500. They frame this as distinct from weak-to-strong generalization.
record.recipe_differences: Human or simulated-human solutions/process labels on easy tasks train generators and reward models; the reward models rerank or optimize generation on hard tasks. No weaker-model labels, weak supervisor baseline, or PGR calculation.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with dataset, RL method, whether RL uses easy or all questions, model size, task difficulty, and reward-model/evaluation setup. The authors state that coding reranking gains differ across hard categories and that reward-model effects are more pronounced on harder math problems.

fits_no_version.finding: An easy-trained 7b OPRM used for weighted-voting reranking still improves a 34b generator's accuracy over majority voting (Fig. 5, Fig. 13). The authors say the 7b evaluator 'can still improve the performance of the 34b generator'. This is a smaller reward model guiding a larger model at inference by reranking, not fine-tuning on weak labels, and no PGR is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A smaller reward model trained on easy tasks can improve a larger generator's hard-task accuracy through reranking.

fits_no_version.finding: In Table 2, RL from an easy-trained PRM on Llemma-7b gives mixed effects on hard-level accuracy. PPO gives modest gains (12.2 to 14.9 on PRM800K). Iterative DPO with All/Easy on MetaMath drops hard accuracy (14.9 to 10.7). These rows measure easy-to-hard transfer, not weak-to-strong supervision.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RL against easy-trained process reward models can improve hard-task accuracy, depending on the RL algorithm and data setup.

fits_no_version.finding: On APPS, a Best-of-16 ORM trained on Introductory problems lifts Code Llama average accuracy over easy-SFT greedy decoding: 15.7 to 18.0 for 7B and 20.1 to 26.6 for 34B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Easy-trained outcome reward models improve reranking on harder coding problems.

record.problems: The study uses a different supervision setup from the claim and does not report PGR. The paper notes focus on specific model sizes and datasets, domain specificity, and the need for further robustness research. No numerical uncertainty is stated for the Table 2 or Table 3 values; figure variance is described for some reranking plots.
record.rows_left_out: Did not extract the many additional decoding-count, model-pair, reward-model-type, aggregation-function, category, and difficulty-level results shown in Figures 4-20 and appendices, nor the full set of Table 1 generator results. These concern the paper's distinct easy-to-hard setup and do not test a listed claim version; figure values are largely presented as plots.

untested.parts: No strong model fine-tuned on weaker-model labels; no weak baseline or PGR.
No training change compared against naive weak-to-strong fine-tuning.
Varies model size, task and reward-model type for easy-to-hard transfer, not PGR against supervisor or student size.
No tests of exploiting unchecked supervisor errors, of distribution shift in weak-to-strong PGR, or of shared weak/strong errors.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly linked to no version. Their states (cannot_determine) are acceptable because no row measures any version's quantity. Hard-level SFT values in Table 2 (12.2 and 14.9) are the easy-to-hard SFT baselines, so the row baselines are read correctly.

versions.untested_parts: No weaker-model supervisor, weak-to-strong student comparison, or PGR measurement.
No training change to weak-to-strong fine-tuning or comparison of its PGR.
The paper varies task, model size, and reward-model setup in easy-to-hard generalization, not PGR or weak-supervisor/student relationships.
No tests of weak-supervisor blind spots, weak-to-strong distribution shift, or shared errors between weak and strong models.
No theory of when a student must beat its supervisor.

relation.reason: The introduction and related work explicitly distinguish easy-to-hard generalization from weak-to-strong generalization; section 3.5 discusses PGR without measuring it.

tranche.reason: The study tests transfer from easy-task supervision to hard tasks, without testing stronger students fine-tuned on weaker supervisors' labels or performance relative to those supervisors.

source_check.notes: The authors-conclusion paraphrase matches the abstract and discussion. These results measure easy-to-hard transfer, so cannot_determine is appropriate for the catalog's weak-to-strong claim versions.
